beats.intro: Lesson sixteen. [[sub]]Why nearly every organization ends up a hybrid, and who has to make it work.
beats.press: To show that hybrids are inevitable, Grove quotes a press release from a trade paper, with the names changed. [[young]]A three-year-old technology company has reorganized into three product divisions. [[heads]]Each is led by a former head of something else: one of the founders, who ran engineering, the former head of sales and marketing, and the former manager of product design. [[keep]]The divisions take on product marketing and product development. [[stay]]But sales and manufacturing stay at the corporate level, serving all three. [[why]]The pattern is the one we just studied. As the product line grew, there was more to keep track of, so each product line got its own organization, while the big functions stayed central.
beats.law: Grove turns this into a law. [[law]]All large organizations with a common business purpose end up in a hybrid form. [[ex]]The breakfast factory, an army, Intel and this young company all fit.
beats.everywhere: And it goes well beyond business. [[school]]A school or university has mission-oriented departments, such as mathematics, English and engineering, and an administration of personnel, security and library services that supplies what every department needs. [[ja]]Junior Achievement is a hybrid too. Each local chapter runs its own little business: it picks a product and sells it. Yet the national organization sets how those businesses are structured, the paperwork, and the rewards for success. [[law2]]Size doesn't decide it either. A friend of Grove's worked at a medium-sized law firm, where lawyers clashed over shared resources such as the stenography pool and office space. [[comm]]They formed an executive committee. It stays out of each attorney's legal work, and handles only getting and sharing the common resources. A small firm, and a hybrid.
beats.q1: Quick check. Mission unit or shared function?
beats.except: Is there any exception? [[cong]]Grove can think of one: the conglomerate. It is usually totally mission-oriented. [[why]]Why? Because it has no common business purpose. Its divisions, or companies, are unrelated, joined only by the profit and loss statement. [[inside]]But look inside any one of those businesses, and you will likely find a hybrid again.
beats.shift: Every hybrid is unique, because there are endless points between the two extremes. [[move]]And an organization can move back and forth along that line, for practical reasons. [[big]]A company with a weak computer buys a big, powerful one. Now centralizing makes sense, for the economies of scale. [[small]]Another replaces a large computer with small, cheap ones that sit in each mission unit, with no loss of scale. [[mgr]]But the most important reason to move should be this: to match the styles and abilities of the managers running the units.
beats.alloc: Sooner or later every large company faces the hybrid's central problem. [[task]]Allocate shared resources well and on time, and settle the conflicts that allocation creates. [[central]]Is the answer allocators in a central office? No. [[hung]]Grove once lived in Hungary, where a central planning office decided what goods would be made, when, and where. [[film]]He was an amateur photographer. Every winter, when he needed high-contrast film, there was none anywhere. [[summer]]Every summer, everyone was up to their waist in it, while ordinary film ran short. [[year]]Year after year, the planners could not respond even to changes in demand that anyone could predict.
beats.load: In theory, a company's top management allocates shared resources and reconciles the units' conflicting needs. [[heavy]]In practice, the transaction load is far too heavy for one place. [[intel]]If Intel tried to settle every conflict and allocate every resource at the top, Grove says, it would start to look like the planners who ran Hungary's economy.
beats.middle: So the answer lies with middle managers. [[many]]First, there are enough of them to cover the whole range of the operation. [[close]]Second, they are very close to the problem: they both generate the company's internal resources and use them. [[two]]To succeed at this high-leverage task, middle managers need two things. [[accept]]They must accept that the hybrid form is inevitable, so they can serve it. [[dual]]And they must master the practice that makes a hybrid manageable: dual reporting. That is the next lesson.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Grove's Law: large organizations with a common purpose end up hybrid. [[w2]]Schools, Junior Achievement and small law firms show it too. [[w3]]The only exception is the conglomerate, with no common purpose. [[w4]]Shift along the line to fit the tools and, above all, the managers. [[w5]]Central planners can't carry the load. Middle managers must. Now the lesson practice.
